cover.html:
⏱ 1:00 · running 0:00 → 1:00

Welcome. Today is about one change in how a SOC runs: moving from a queue that waits for people to a platform that works the queue and brings people decisions.

The cube on the right is the story of the talk: the platform is Elastic Security, the coloured cubes are the queue (alerts, hunts, rules), and the pink cube is AlertZero sweeping across it. Work keeps arriving; it keeps getting worked.

⏱ 1:00 · running 1:00 → 2:00

Five chapters. The deep dive is chapter 3, how AlertZero actually works: Watches, Workers and the hand-offs between them. Chapter 4 is the part security leaders care most about: how you stay in control. Then we see it run, live.

About 40 minutes of talk, then the demo and questions.

attacker.html:

Start with the attacker, because AI changed their economics first.

▸ click 1 · 80–90%: building custom malware costs a fraction of what it did. What needed a skilled team now needs a prompt.
▸ click 2 · 100+ CVEs a month, 6 zero-days patched in February alone. Manual patch cycles can't keep pace.
▸ click 3 · +42% more zero-days exploited before disclosure. Agents fuzz and find vulnerabilities on their own.
▸ click 4 · Every 7 minutes a new vulnerability is published. September 2026 Patch Tuesday: 966 fixes in one release. Let the clock run for a moment.

Transition: attackers scaled with AI. Now look at what that does to the analyst.
analyst.html:
⏱ 2:30 · running 4:30 → 7:00

Four things analysts tell us, in their words.

▸ click 1 · Alert fatigue: "I can't trust my own queue." The real attack is buried in noise.
▸ click 2 · Intel lag: "The blog dropped Tuesday, we're still building coverage." Research to detection is manual.
▸ click 3 · Investigation toil: correlating endpoint, cloud and identity by hand takes all afternoon.
▸ click 4 · No trust in AI: a confident answer with no receipts is worse than none. Remember this one; chapter 4 answers it.
▸ click 5 · The numbers: days from blog to coverage, thousands of alerts a shift, five-plus data planes.
overnight.html:
⏱ 1:30 · running 7:00 → 8:30

So ask a different question: what if the queue never waited for a person?

Illustrative overnight volume: 1,859 items. Not just alerts: hunts, rule proposals, investigations, actions.

▸ click 1 · Watch them get worked: each one closed with a reason, or folded into a decision. The counter shows what is still waiting.
▸ click 2 · One needs a person. It arrives as a proposal with the evidence attached.
▸ click 3 · Closed with a reason, or folded into one decision, before anyone arrived. That is the promise of AlertZero.
platform.html:
⏱ 1:30 · running 8:30 → 10:00

Before AlertZero itself: where it runs. It is not a new silo.

▸ click 1 · Elasticsearch: every signal at retention. This is the evidence every Worker reads.
▸ click 2 · Workflows: AlertZero's Workers are ordinary Elastic Workflows. Elastic installs, manages and upgrades them.

fronts.html:
⏱ 1:00 · running 10:00 → 11:00

introducing.html:
⏱ 1:30 · running 14:00 → 15:30

Introducing AlertZero: the agentic layer of Elastic Security. Every alert, every rule, every hunt, worked around the clock, with a human on the loop. Not in the loop doing the work: on the loop, making the calls.

It is organised as four Watches around your SOC.
▸ click 1 · Triage Watch: every alert, before you see it.
▸ click 2 · Hunt Watch: hunting that never sleeps.
▸ click 3 · Detection Watch: fix the rule, not the symptom.
▸ click 4 · Forensics Watch: deep research on a host.
watch.html:
⏱ 1:30 · running 15:30 → 17:00

What is a Watch? A named team of agents with one job, on duty around the clock, reporting to your people.

▸ click 1 · The four Watches.
▸ click 2 · The Workers inside each one, with their schedules: Alert Triage every 15 minutes, Attack Discovery daily, the hunt every 4 hours, coverage hourly, tuning every 2 hours, and Endpoint Analysis polling every minute.
▸ click 3 · What flows: proposals with evidence go up (yellow); bounds and autonomy come down (blue).
▸ click 4 · The vocabulary: a Watch is a group plus a settings page; a Worker owns schedule, autonomy and budget; the shared workflow holds the logic and is managed by Elastic.
watch-flow.html:
- Keys on this slide: Enter (or click) approve / continue, [ ] previous / next chapter, 1-7 jump to a chapter, S start over, A auto-run, P presenter mode. The two approvals are where the person in the room is the human in the loop.
- 1 Intake: every alert gets worked. Most of it is noise, and it closes with a reason a person can read, not a silent drop.
- 2 Feedback to Detection: Triage Watch sees the same rule close as noise again and again and hands the pattern to Detection Watch, which proposes a fix with a backtest. Nothing ships until someone approves. Watch the flood thin once it does.
- 3 Escalation: the credential-misuse alerts escalate. Triage Watch uses Attack Discovery to group related activity and opens one Investigation: entities, a timeline, how far it has spread. The Investigation is the shared record every Watch adds to.
- 4 Forensics depth: when Triage cannot explain an unknown binary, the request goes to Forensics Watch. It pulls the file through Elastic Defend and writes a verdict and the C2 domain into the same Investigation.
- 5 Response: Forensics Watch stages a Proposal, not an action: isolate the host, disable the account, block the domain. It waits for a person at every autonomy setting.
- 6 Hunt loop: Hunt Watch takes the indicators and technique and sweeps the estate. It finds two more hosts, adds them to the Investigation, and gives Detection Watch a new rule idea.
- 7 Close: three thousand alerts, six human decisions. You set how far each Watch goes on its own. Changing that never changes what is included.
worker.html:
⏱ 2:00 · running 17:00 → 19:00

Every Worker has the same shape. Learn it once and you understand all six.

▸ click 1 · A trigger starts the per-space Worker, which calls the shared workflow. The workflow gathers the evidence: alerts, entities, raw events.
▸ click 2 · One AI step. The key design choice: the model has no tools. Evidence goes in the prompt; a verdict and reasons come out. Predictable cost, predictable results.
▸ click 3 · The result is journaled in an Investigation, and any change becomes a Proposal that waits at a gate, up to 72 hours.
▸ click 4 · Approved, an action workflow makes the change, running as the person who approved it. Watch the work item travel and stop at the gate until a person says yes.
handoffs.html:
⏱ 2:00 · running 19:00 → 21:00

How work moves between Watches. They never call each other directly; they hand off through data.

Walk the lanes briefly: hunt, detection, triage, forensics. Pink border = a model call, yellow shadow = a proposal.
▸ click 1 · The hunt finds a detection gap and writes a coverage indicator. Rule Coverage picks it up.
▸ click 2 · Alerts closed as false positives (by you or by triage) teach Rule Tuning which rules are noisy.
▸ click 3 · Approving a forensics hand-off writes an analyze_endpoint indicator; Endpoint Analysis sees it within a minute.
▸ click 4 · The consequence: turn any Worker off and nothing breaks. The work just waits.
triage.html:
⏱ 2:00 · running 21:00 → 23:00

Triage Watch in detail.

▸ click 1 · Alert Triage claims a fair batch per rule within a 1,300 an hour budget. The claim tag stops two sweeps taking the same alert.
▸ click 2 · One verdict per alert, written back as a tag and a note with reasons. Nothing closed yet.
▸ click 3 · Confident false positives, 0.85 and above, become one proposal per rule: close 15 alerts. Dismiss it and they return to the queue.
▸ click 4 · Attack Discovery runs four checks on every attack. Note the inconclusive verdict: a missing signal is treated as unknown, never as a false positive. That honesty is a design rule.
hunt-shift.html:
⏱ 1:30 · running 23:00 → 24:30

Hunt Watch: from reacting to a queue to a hunt that runs for you. Five shifts.

▸ click 1 · Reading the blog and building by hand becomes intel turned into validated detection.
▸ click 2 · Someone clicking hunt becomes an always-on sweep, with schema-aware ES|QL that is dry-run before it runs.
▸ click 3 · Every alert demanding attention becomes a finding only on a real hit.
▸ click 4 · An afternoon of correlation becomes campaigns assembled across endpoint, cloud and identity.
▸ click 5 · Trusting a black box becomes receipts on every finding, and rules that deploy disabled.
hunt-pipeline.html:
⏱ 1:30 · running 24:30 → 26:00

Inside one hunt, using the axios supply-chain report as the example.

▸ click 1 · The report is ingested and enriched: the model pulls out the indicators (yellow) and the tradecraft (pink).
▸ click 2 · Tier 1 searches the indicators. Zero hits: a less honest tool would stop here and say you're clean.
▸ click 3 · Tier 2 writes a behaviour query from the report text against your real mappings, and dry-runs it first.
▸ click 4 · A real hit: one build runner ran node → sh → curl during CI.
▸ click 5 · Two proposals: isolate the host, and draft a rule for the gap, created disabled.
detection.html:
⏱ 1:30 · running 26:00 → 27:30

Detection Watch: fix the rule, not the symptom.

▸ click 1 · Rule Coverage reads the gap the hunt found.
▸ click 2 · Cheapest fix first: is there a disabled rule to enable? A prebuilt rule to install? Only then draft a new ES|QL rule, previewed and created disabled.
▸ click 3 · Rule Tuning watches for rules with 10+ false positives or a 50% false-positive rate over 7 days.
▸ click 4 · It proposes an exception and backtests it with a rule preview: same run, old vs new alert counts.
▸ click 5 · And rule changes always ask a person, at every autonomy level.
forensics.html:
⏱ 1:30 · running 27:30 → 29:00

Forensics Watch: deep research, then one decision per action.

▸ click 1 · Endpoint Analysis picks up the approved hand-off within a minute.
▸ click 2 · The forensic agent rebuilds the host timeline: from the zip in Outlook to the outbound connection, with a verdict.
▸ click 3 · Findings and IoCs are filed in the same Investigation, so the story stays in one place.
▸ click 4 · One proposal per containment action. Close Investigation always asks. Containment runs through Elastic Defend.
proposals.html:
⏱ 1:30 · running 29:00 → 30:30

Chapter 4, trust and control. The core idea: proposals, not alerts.

▸ click 1 · The machine is always on: reads the intel, hunts, builds the evidence, proposes. Everything it does is a proposal.
▸ click 2 · The hand-off: completed work arrives with evidence, provenance and the query. The analyst reviews receipts, makes the call, and sets the dial.
▸ click 3 · Every decision feeds back. Approvals and rejections re-rank what gets hunted next: your judgement trains the queue.
autonomy.html:
⏱ 2:00 · running 30:30 → 32:30

You set how far it goes, per Watch.

▸ click 1 · Manual, the default: it suggests, you approve every step.
▸ click 2 · Assisted: it investigates; closing and response wait for you.
▸ click 3 · Supervised: approved classes of action finish end to end, and you can undo.
▸ click 4 · Some actions always ask, at every level: closing an Investigation, and any rule change.
▸ click 5 · At supervised, these can auto-approve: closing confident false positives, forensics hand-offs, and containment on scheduled runs only. A manual run of Endpoint Analysis always stays manual.

Suggest customers start on manual and earn their way up.
receipts.html:
⏱ 1:30 · running 32:30 → 34:00

Back to the analyst who asked "why should I believe the model?" Every finding carries its receipts.

▸ click 1 · Evidence first, model only judges, no tools. Alert IDs the model invents are dropped. The receipt shows evidence, query and model.
▸ click 2 · Approved actions run as the approver. Proposals expire after 72 hours rather than vanish. The receipt adds verdict, reasons and the proposal.
▸ click 3 · Guardrails: one sweep per space, hard budgets, back-pressure. And the honest no: unknown stays unknown, zero stays zero. Approved, ran as a human, audited.

▸ click 2 · Midnight: the hunt runs the axios report and finds one real hit. Isolation waits.
▸ click 3 · 01:00: the coverage gap becomes a disabled draft rule.
▸ click 4 · 02:00: scanner noise gets an exception, backtested.
▸ click 5 · 04:00: Attack Discovery finds one real attack; the hand-off auto-approves.
▸ click 6 · 04:01: Endpoint Analysis rebuilds the timeline. Isolation waits for a person.
▸ click 7 · 08:00: coffee, and six decisions, each with receipts.
scenarios.html:
⏱ 2:00 · running 36:00 → 38:00

The demo runs four real threat reports through the hunt. Four honest answers.

▸ click 1 · A, axios: found in our environment. Our own build runner installed it.
▸ click 2 · B, stolen CI credentials: the keys that RAT harvested show up in AWS. Same campaign, second stage.
▸ click 3 · C, Okta help desk: real hits, but a different actor. The hunt refuses to connect it.
▸ click 4 · D, edge appliances we don't run: matched nothing, wrote nothing. The quiet control.
▸ click 5 · The links: A and B correlated, C explicitly not, D silent. The honest no is the trust signal. Same pipeline every time.
demo.html:

Switch to the live environment after the clicks.

▸ click 1 · The queue is decisions: overnight, every alert triaged with reasoning; six rows need a person.
▸ click 2 · Approve, and Defend acts: one yes isolates the host, one yes tunes the noisy rule. Two rows turn green.

Why this works on Elastic.

▸ click 1 · One data foundation: years of history and one query across cloud, on-prem and edge. Workers read the same evidence as your analysts.
▸ click 2 · Open and sovereign: our model or yours, including local and air-gapped. Watch the model slot swap: nothing else changes.

takeaways.html:
⏱ 1:00 · running 40:00 → 41:00

Three things to remember.

▸ click 1 · The SOC hits bottlenecks everywhere. We covered two answers on one platform.
▸ click 2 · Prevention cuts the alert load at the source.
▸ click 3 · AlertZero works the rest, and you stay in command: you see the query and the evidence and approve every consequential action.
▸ click 4 · Read the closing line.
